meta.title: Tokenisation for Issuers: VDEP, MDES, and the Decisions That Matter | Panasa
meta.description: Every cardholder payment now travels as a token, not a real card number. A practical guide to VDEP, MDES, provisioning, and the tokenisation decisions every card program must get right.

title: Tokenisation for Issuers: VDEP, MDES, and the Decisions That Matter
author: Fathima Roshni

body.content:
Every time a cardholder pays online or taps their phone at a terminal, their actual card number stays out of the transaction entirely. What travels instead is a token: a unique digital substitute for the real card number. This process is called Tokenisation, and it has quietly become the security layer present in most digital payments.

The numbers tell the story. Visa reported over 11.5 billion active tokens by the end of 2024. Nearly half of Mastercard's e-commerce transactions in Europe are already tokenised. Networks argue tokens cut online payment fraud by up to 60%. For a card program, Tokenisation is no longer a feature to consider. It is the foundation your cardholders expect.

What is Tokenisation?

Tokenisation replaces the sixteen-digit sensitive card number, the Primary Account Number (PAN) printed on a physical card, with a unique digital identifier called a token or DPAN (Device Primary Account Number). The actual card details are never shared during the transaction. The token is what travels instead.

When a cardholder adds their card to Apple Pay, Google Pay, or Samsung Pay, they are not storing their real card number on the device. They are storing a DPAN, generated by the card network and mapped to the real PAN. The DPAN is device-specific and revocable. If it is compromised, the issuer revokes the token and generates a new one without reissuing the physical card. The same logic applies to card-on-file tokens stored by merchants for recurring transactions. Each token is merchant-specific, so a breach at one merchant does not expose the cardholder's credentials elsewhere.

body.content:
How Tokenisation Works

Three parties are involved in every Tokenisation request: the token requestor (Apple, Google, or a merchant), the token service provider (Visa or Mastercard), and the issuer host, which is the processor on the issuer's side that approves or declines the request.

When a cardholder registers their card with a mobile wallet, the following happens:

  1. The token requestor sends a request to the token service provider.
  2. The token service provider sends a Token Activation Request (TAR) to the issuer host.
  3. The issuer host approves or declines. This is your program's decision point.
  4. If approved, the token service provider generates DPAN and notifies the requestor.
  5. The token appears on the cardholder's device, ready to use.

VDEP and MDES: The Two Programs Your Card Program Needs to Know

Both Visa and Mastercard run separate Tokenisation services. Mastercard's is called MDES, the Mastercard Digital Enablement Service. Visa's is called VTS, the Visa Token Service, accessed through a commercial framework known as VDEP, the Visa Digital Enablement Program. They do the same job: generate tokens and manage the token lifecycle. But they are separate integrations. A dual-scheme card program needs to be enrolled in both.

VDEP gives issuers access to all Visa token requesters through a single connection at no per-token fee, removing the need to negotiate individual agreements with Apple, Google, Samsung, and every card-on-file merchant separately. MDES provides the equivalent framework for Mastercard. Your processor handles the technical integration with both, but the program manager needs to know which BIN ranges are enrolled and whether auto-enrolment is active across all live cards.

body.content:
Card Provisioning: How Tokenisation Reaches Your Cardholder's Wallet

Enrolling in VDEP and MDES sets up the tokenisation infrastructure. Provisioning determines how that token reaches your cardholder's device. It is the process of delivering a token to a digital wallet, so the cardholder can actually use it. Without provisioning, the tokenisation setup has nowhere to go.

There are technically two provisioning paths. Manual provisioning exists, where the cardholder opens their wallet app and enters card details by hand, but in practice this rarely happens. Push provisioning, where the cardholder taps "Add to Wallet" inside your banking app and the card is provisioned instantly, is now the expected experience.

Push provisioning requires additional integration between your issuer processor and the wallet provider. It is not automatic. But it directly affects activation rates, wallet adoption, and top-of-wallet positioning. A card that provisions instantly gets used first. A card that requires manual entry often does not get added at all.

What Tokenisation Means for Your Issuing Strategy

The program that gets Tokenisation right early benefits from several advantages like higher authorisation rates, lower fraud losses, fewer physical card reissues when credentials are compromised, and cardholder behavior anchored around their preferred wallet. The program that delays it finds their cards sitting as backup methods rather than primary ones. Networks have signaled the eventual decline of static PAN transactions. Visa and Mastercard are already moving toward token-only checkout flows in key markets.

Conclusion

Tokenisation is not a separate workstream from card program design. It is part of it. Which BIN ranges are enrolled matters. Whether push provisioning is active matters. How the program handles token lifecycle events such as card expiry, replacement, and fraud triggered revocation matters. Each of these is a card program's decision with direct consequences for cardholder experience and fraud exposure. The programs that think through these early, run more stable, lose less, and keep their card at the front of the wallet.
